inlines.text: Each pair of variables has a correlation.
Which ones are likely to have a
Ice cream sales and number of sunburns reported
Reading skills of children and shoe size
Number of books in a home and family income
Number of cashiers and average checkout time in a supermarket
Number of patients in a hospital emergency room and waiting time
Number of computers and number of TVs in a home
Loan interest rate and size of monthly repayments
Driving speed of a vehicle and time taken to arrive home
Maths test mark and English test mark
Number of storks and birth rate in a region
Proportion of smokers in a population and incidence of lung cancer
Social media use and short attention spans

answer.short: A, E, F, H, I, L.
answer.worked:
A: Warmer weather can increase demand for ice cream.

E: More cashiers can reduce checkout time when customer demand is unchanged.

F: More patients can increase waiting time when staffing is unchanged.

H: A higher interest rate increases repayments for the same loan amount and repayment term.

I: A higher average speed reduces travel time over the same distance.

L: Smoking increases the risk of lung cancer.

These pairs have plausible causal mechanisms; correlation alone does not establish causation.

Correct answer: A, E, F, H, I, L.

sections.title: Drawing a line of best fit

inlines.text: Represents most of the points as closely as possible.
Follows the overall trend; it does not need to pass through any particular data point.
Has roughly the same number of points above and below it.
Is drawn so that the distances of points from the line are as small as possible.
extend the line past existing data points, as the relationship may not continue outside of this range.
A line of best fit may not “fit” the data nicely if there is an outlier.
A line of best fit calculated using a statistical method is called a
line. It can be calculated using a computer.

For students who missed no lessons, the highest score is $100$ and the lowest is $80$.

inlines.text: it takes a number of students to swim 25 m freestyle is recorded in the table.
Give the correlation coefficient and regression coefficients to 2 decimal places. Use age in years as the explanatory variable.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Pearson’s correlation coefficient $r$

answer.worked:
Enter age as $x$ and time as $y$ in two-variable statistics mode. Select linear regression and read Pearson's correlation coefficient.
$$\begin{align*}r&=-0.2551259466\\r&\approx-0.26\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: The equation of the line of best fit $y=a+bx$

answer.short: $y=30.35-0.23x$, where $x$ is age in years and $y$ is time in seconds.
answer.worked:
Using linear regression with age as $x$ and time as $y$:
$$\begin{align*}a&=30.3479452055\\b&=-0.2301369863\\y&\approx30.35-0.23x\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: Identify the strength and direction of the association.

answer.worked: $r\approx-0.26$ is negative and lies in the weak negative range on the supplied correlation scale.

children.prompt: Interpret the gradient and $y$-intercept.

answer.short: Each additional year of age is associated with an estimated decrease of 0.23 s in swimming time. The intercept gives a formal model time of 30.35 s at age 0; it is outside the observed ages and is not a realistic prediction.
answer.worked:
The gradient is approximately $-0.23$ seconds per year, so the estimated time to swim 25 m tends to decrease by 0.23 s for each additional year of age.

At $x=0$, the model gives $y=30.35$ s. This is the formal intercept, but age 0 is outside the observed range of 11–26 years, so it has no realistic predictive interpretation here.

inlines.text: The results of a group of students on Mathematics and Science tests are compared.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the equation of the regression line predicting Science score $S$ from Mathematics score $M$. Give the coefficients to 2 decimal places.

answer.worked:
Enter Mathematics scores as $x$ and Science scores as $y$ in the calculator's two-variable statistics mode. Select linear regression $y=a+bx$.
$$\begin{align*}a&=8.004145\ldots\\b&=0.927461\ldots\\S&\approx8.00+0.93M\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Using the rounded equation from part a, predict the score in Science of a student who scores 80 in Mathematics. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}S&=8.00+0.93(80)\\S&=82.4\end{align*}$$
The estimated Science score is $82.4$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Using the rounded equation from part a, predict the score in Mathematics of a student who scores 60 in Science. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}60&=8.00+0.93M\\0.93M&=52\\M&=\frac{52}{0.93}\\M&\approx55.9\end{align*}$$
The estimated Mathematics score is $55.9$. This extrapolated estimate is less reliable because it is outside the observed data range.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Is part b or c an example of extrapolation?

answer.short: Part c: a Science score of $60$ is outside the observed range $68$–$89$.
answer.worked: Part b uses a Mathematics score of $80$, within the observed Mathematics range $64$–$85$, so it is interpolation. Part c uses a Science score of $60$, below the observed Science range $68$–$89$, so it is extrapolation.

inlines.text: The data shows the average height of 17-year-old girls from 1850 to 1990.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Pearson’s correlation coefficient $r$ (to 5 decimal places)

answer.worked:
Enter years in A2:A9 and heights in B2:B9. Use the spreadsheet formula =CORREL(A2:A9,B2:B9).

$r = 0.982640459\ldots \approx 0.98264$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Strength and direction

answer.worked: $r$ is positive and lies between $0.75$ and $1$, so the association is strong positive.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Equation of the line of best fit $y = mx + c$ (gradient to 4 decimal places and intercept to 2 decimal places)

answer.worked:
Create a scatter chart with year as $x$ and height in centimetres as $y$. Add a linear trendline and display its equation.

$y = 0.152380952\ldots x - 134.571428571\ldots$

To the requested precision, $y = 0.1524x - 134.57$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Interpret the gradient and $y$-intercept

answer.short: Average height tends to increase by approximately $0.1524$ cm per year. The intercept gives a formal model height of $-134.57$ cm at year $0$; this has no realistic interpretation.
answer.worked:
The gradient is approximately $0.1524$ cm per year, so the model estimates that average height of 17-year-old girls increases by this amount each year over the observed period.

At $x = 0$, the model gives $y \approx -134.57$ cm. Year $0$ is far outside 1850–1990 and a negative height is impossible, so the intercept is a formal model value with no realistic predictive meaning.

sourceAtom.label: Investigation
sourceAtom.visibleSubtitle: Height and armspan

content.prompt: Measure the height and armspan of the students in your class (separate results for males and females) and record the information in a table (or directly into a spreadsheet).

children.label: a
children.prompt: Draw a scatterplot of the data using a spreadsheet.

answer.short: Plots depend on the collected data. Put height (cm) on the horizontal axis and armspan (cm) on the vertical axis.
answer.worked: Enter paired height and armspan measurements in two spreadsheet columns, keeping separate datasets for males and females. For each dataset, select both columns and insert an XY scatterplot with height (cm) on the horizontal axis and armspan (cm) on the vertical axis. Plot one point for each student.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Calculate the value of $r$. Describe the correlation between these two variables in terms of direction (positive/negative) and strength (perfect/strong/moderate/weak).

answer.short: Answers depend on the data. Calculate $r$ separately for males and females and describe each correlation using its sign and the taught strength scale.
answer.worked: For each dataset, use the spreadsheet formula =CORREL(height_range,armspan_range), selecting corresponding numerical cells and excluding the headers. Positive $r$ indicates a positive association; negative $r$ indicates a negative association. Use the taught scale: $|r|<0.25$ indicates no meaningful linear relationship, $0.25\leq|r|<0.50$ weak, $0.50\leq|r|<0.75$ moderate, $0.75\leq|r|<1$ strong, and $|r|=1$ perfect. Report each calculated value and its description.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Is one variable a good predictor of the other?

answer.short: Data-dependent: a strong linear association supports useful predictions; a weak or near-zero correlation does not.
answer.worked: Consider each scatterplot and its value of $r$. If the points lie close to a straight line and $|r|$ is close to 1, height is a useful predictor of armspan within the observed range. If the points are widely scattered or $r$ is near zero, predictions are less reliable.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Use technology to add the least-squares regression line of best fit to the data.

answer.short: Add a linear least-squares trendline to each spreadsheet scatterplot.
answer.worked: Select each scatterplot and add a linear trendline. Choose Format trendline and Display equation on chart. With height $x$ and armspan $y$, record the fitted equation $y=a+bx$. The coefficients depend on the collected data.

children.label: e
children.prompt: Interpret the gradient and $y$ intercept of your trendline.

answer.short: For $y=a+bx$, $b$ is the estimated change in armspan (cm) for each additional centimetre of height. The intercept $a$ is the formal predicted armspan at height 0 cm and has no realistic interpretation here.
answer.worked: For each fitted equation $y=a+bx$, the gradient $b$ means that armspan tends to change by $b$ cm for every 1 cm increase in height. The $y$ intercept $a$ is the model's predicted armspan when height is 0 cm. This lies outside the observed heights and is not a realistic prediction for a person.

children.label: f
children.prompt: Mr Ding has a height of 181 cm. Predict his armspan. Give your estimate to 2 decimal places.

answer.short: Using the male-student model $y=a+bx$, his estimated armspan is $a+181b$ cm, rounded to 2 decimal places.
answer.worked:
Use the male-student regression equation, retaining the fitted coefficients' available precision.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=a+bx\\y&=a+b(181)\end{aligned}$$
Evaluate and round the estimated armspan to 2 decimal places, in centimetres.

children.label: g
children.prompt: Compare your prediction to his actual armspan. Is his armspan shorter or longer than expected?

answer.short: Measure his actual armspan. It is longer than expected if actual minus predicted is positive, and shorter if it is negative.
answer.worked:
Let $A$ be Mr Ding's measured armspan and $P$ the prediction from part f, both in centimetres.
$$\text{difference}=A-P$$
A positive difference means his armspan is longer than expected; a negative difference means it is shorter. A zero difference means it matches the prediction. His actual armspan must be measured before a numerical comparison can be made.

children.label: h
children.prompt: Comment on the validity of your model.

answer.short: Validity depends on the linear association, scatter, outliers, measurement quality and whether Mr Ding is comparable to the sampled students. Predictions outside the sampled height range are less reliable.
answer.worked: Use the scatterplot and $r$ to assess whether a linear model is suitable. Discuss outliers, the number of students and measurement accuracy. Check whether 181 cm lies within the sampled heights; otherwise the prediction is extrapolation. Mr Ding is an adult, so a model based on students may not apply as well to him. Compare the prediction with his measured armspan and explain what that difference suggests about this prediction's reliability.

sourceAtom.label: Investigation
sourceAtom.visibleSubtitle: Storks deliver babies?

inlines.text: A familiar folk tale is that storks deliver babies, used by parents since ancient times to avoid answering the awkward question “where do babies come from?”
We will investigate whether there is a correlation between storks and birth rate.
Estimated stork population data is available for 17 European countries, shown in the table. We will compare this to the number of human births per year.

children.label: a

children.prompt: Complete the sentences.

answer.worked: Correlation does not necessarily imply causation. An observed association alone does not establish that one variable causes the other.

answer.worked: Country area is a possible confounding factor: larger countries can support more storks and have more births. The correlations suggest this explanation but do not by themselves prove a causal mechanism.

arrangements.description: Continuation of the existing investigation, without a new activity heading. Scatterplots are created in Excel; coefficients and sentence completions use native dotted clozes.

inlines.text: Read the article and answer the questions:

In the stork investigation, countries with more storks tended to have more births per year. This does not mean that storks deliver babies. Country area is a possible confounding variable. Larger countries can have more rural land, where storks are more common, and larger populations, resulting in more births. This illustrates a spurious correlation: two things that appear related without a cause-and-effect link between them.
Correlation does not imply causation. Two things can occur together without either one causing the other.

A common modern example is the claim that violent video games cause aggressive behaviour. If a study finds a correlation between playing these games and aggression, other factors such as temperament or home environment may explain both the game choice and the behaviour. The correlation alone doesn’t establish cause.

In the 1950s, tobacco companies used the same logic when scientists first linked smoking to lung cancer. They argued the relationship might be spurious, just like storks and birth rates. This delayed public understanding of the risk for years.
So how did scientists eventually establish that smoking does cause lung cancer?
They used several independent lines of evidence:
Large-scale studies showed smokers had far higher rates of lung cancer than non-smokers.
Laboratory experiments showed cigarette smoke damages DNA and causes mutations.
Lung cancer risk fell in people who quit smoking.
Animals exposed to cigarette smoke developed lung cancer.
existed: more smoking meant higher risk.
No single piece of evidence was enough on its own. Taken together, they established a causal relationship.
Distinguishing correlation from causation matters in science, policy, and everyday life. Confusing the two is a common feature of misleading arguments.

children.prompt: What is a spurious correlation? Use the stork example in your answer.

answer.short: An association without a causal link between the variables. Stork counts and annual birth totals may both be related to country area.
answer.worked: A spurious correlation occurs when two variables are associated without either causing the other. In the stork example, larger countries may have more storks and more births. Country area is a possible confounding variable; storks do not cause births.

children.prompt: Tobacco companies argued that the link between smoking and lung cancer might be spurious. Why was this argument flawed?

answer.short: A possible confounder does not refute causation. Multiple independent lines of evidence supported a causal link.
answer.worked: Correlation alone would not establish causation, but suggesting a possible alternative explanation did not refute the other evidence. Laboratory evidence, lower risk after quitting, animal studies and a dose-response relationship together supported a causal link between smoking and lung cancer.

children.prompt: Two students are discussing violent video games. One says: “Studies show that people who play violent video games are more aggressive, so the games must be causing the aggression.” What is wrong with this reasoning?

answer.short: The student confuses correlation with causation. Other factors could explain both game choice and aggression.
answer.worked: An observed correlation does not establish that the games cause aggression. Temperament or home environment could influence both the choice of games and aggressive behaviour. Further evidence is needed to establish causation.

taughtMethods: Consider independent lines of causal evidence

entries.description:
Syllabus Content
MA5-DAT-C-02 displays and interprets datasets involving bivariate data

Identify and describe numerical datasets involving 2 variables
• Distinguish between situations involving 1-variable and 2-variable (bivariate) data and explain when each is needed
• Explain the difference between variables that have an association and variables that have a causal relationship
• Identify and describe the independent variable and dependent variable in relationships with possible cause and effect

Represent datasets involving 2 numerical variables, using a scatter plot and a line of best fit, by eye
• Gather data on a topic of interest involving 2 numerical variables
• Represent the data using a scatter plot
• Create a line of best fit, by eye, on an existing scatter plot

Interpret data involving 2 numerical variables, using graphical representations
• Describe informally the association between 2 numerical variables and apply terminology about form (linear), strength (strong, moderate or weak) and direction (positive or negative)
• Use the line of best fit, by eye, to make predictions between known data values (interpolation) and what might happen beyond known data values (extrapolation)
• Explain the limitations of the model when making predictions

entries.description: Bivariate Data

Univariate data counts the frequency of a single variable.
Bivariate data explores relationships between two variables.
The independent variable often causes changes in the dependent variable, but not always.
For example, for a relationship between maths test scores and hours spent on social media,
Mr Ding’s hypothesis might be that more hours on social media mean lower test scores.
• The independent variable would be hours on social media.
• The dependent variable would be maths test score.

entries.description: Drawing a Line of Best Fit

A line of best fit:
• Represents most of the points as closely as possible.
• Goes through as many points as possible.
• Has roughly the same number of points above and below it.
• Is drawn so that the distances of points from the line are as small as possible.

Do NOT extend the line past existing data points, as the relationship may not continue outside of this range.
A line of best fit may not “fit” the data nicely if there is an outlier.

A line of best fit is also referred to as a regression line, if it was generated using a special method using a computer.

entries.description:
Interpolating and Extrapolating using the Equation
We can use the equation of the line to interpolate and extrapolate without using the line itself.
1. Identify the given variable: independent (x) or dependent (y).
2. Substitute the known value into the equation.
3. Solve to find the unknown variable.

entries.description:
In the late 1800s, researchers noticed something odd: places with more storks also had higher birth rates. Storks weren't delivering babies. The confounding variable was area. Larger countries have more rural land, storks are more common in rural areas, and rural families tend to have more children. This is a classic example of a spurious correlation: two things that appear related but have no cause-and-effect link.

Correlation does not imply causation. Two things can occur together without either one causing the other.

A common modern example is the claim that violent video games cause aggressive behaviour. There is a correlation between playing these games and aggression, but other factors such as temperament or home environment may explain both the game choice and the behaviour. The correlation alone doesn't establish cause.

In the 1950s, tobacco companies used the same logic when scientists first linked smoking to lung cancer. They argued the relationship might be spurious, just like storks and birth rates. This delayed public understanding of the risk for years.

So how did scientists eventually establish that smoking does cause lung cancer?

They used several independent lines of evidence:
- Large-scale studies showed smokers had far higher rates of lung cancer than non-smokers.
- Laboratory experiments showed cigarette smoke damages DNA and causes mutations.
- Lung cancer risk fell in people who quit smoking.
- Animals exposed to cigarette smoke developed lung cancer.
- A clear dose-response relationship existed: more smoking meant higher risk.

No single piece of evidence was enough on its own. Taken together, they established a causal relationship.

Distinguishing correlation from causation matters in science, policy, and everyday life, and is a common tool in misleading arguments.
